Judy Van Wyck, Chairperson Africana Studies supports the Department of Sociology in their proposal for a Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities Minor.
The AAF Faculty have several concerns that can be summarized in the following statement.
While we support a minor in social justi ce, we believe the present state of Africana Studies reflects the results of systematic lack of support, marginalization and institutionalized neglect.

Without the adequate funding, staffing and support that is necessary for any area of study to carry out basic administrative and academic functions, successful and progressive development is impeded.
Complexly, Africana Studies has "partnered" in the past with other departments in well-meaning projects.
Often the result has been that the other departments receive the recognition and subsequent funding while Africana Studies remains perpetually without recognition of its contributions and thereby unable to garner the funding and support necessary for progress.
We have seen this pattern repeated too many times and we are hoping that these kinds of institutional blocks to true equity and social justice can be dismantled.
We would like our support of the Social Justice and Civic Responsiblities minor to strengthen increased support of Africana Studies, specifically, adequate funding, staffing and departmental status.

Toward that end, we conditionally support Sociology in the effort to establish a very important minor, the Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities minor, and even expect our relationship with Sociology to model social justice by noting the following concerns: A.) This Minor should not be seen as a segue away from the Africana Studies Major/Minor, but rather a field of study that is compatible with the academic goals of Africana Studies.
B.) Africana Studies will be able to "count" involvement in the Social Justice minor as credit in our overall assessment C.) Africana Studies maintains rightful decision -making over hiring of Faculty (especially adjunct Faculty) to teach the courses that are solely designated as AAF.
D.) The Sociology Department will keep Africana Studies informed of decisions about the minor that will impact Africana Studies.
Sincerely, Dr.

Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities are required to take at least one course from each of three categories of courses (peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills) and not more than three from each category for a total of 18 credits. Students are encouraged to meet with someone from the minor advisory committee or the minor director, Dr. Judy A. Van Wyk in the Department of Sociology & Anthropology before they begin to plan which courses best suit their career and academic goals. With at least 68 courses to choose from, students will gain knowledge and skills that are necessary for our diverse and changing world that are applicable to any career. Courses for the minor are available from African American Studies, Business, Criminology & Criminal Justice, Communications, Economics, Education, English, Gender & Women's Studies, Human Development and Family Studies, History, Latin American Studies, Labor Relations and Human Resources, Marine Affairs, Nursing, Music, Philosophy, Political Science, Psychology, Sociology & Anthropology, and Writing. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Health Sciences is a rapidly changing and evolving discipline, requiring highly trained, critical thinkers to solve some of society’s biggest health-related problems. The Ph.D. in Health Sciences is a college-wide degree with faculty from multiple departments/programs in the College of Health Sciences and focuses on health, wellness, and quality of life across the lifespan. Research brings together faculty and students to solve important health-related problems through a mix of basic, applied and translational science. The program allows students the opportunity to gain experience in the various disciplines that make up health sciences and provides them with the opportunity for advanced content knowledge and in- depth training in one discipline or area of study.

Students are eligible to apply for this program after earning a post-baccalaureate degree in a health-related field. Physical Therapy was not initially included as a specialization because the graduate catalog language (which has now been changed) required a master’s degree to have 30 credits from their post-baccalaureate degree apply to their doctoral program. Physical Therapy does not offer a master's degree. Instead, students in this discipline go on to the

doctoral of physical therapy (DPT).
Therefore, no credits from the DPT would count toward the PhD.
The graduate council approved language (Nov. 9, 2020) in the graduate manual to let students with a master’s or qualifying graduate degree request up to 30 credits from this degree to be applied to their doctoral program.
This includes the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) degree.
Given this change, we would like to add Physical Therapy as a specialization to the CHS doctoral program.
